strengths: AVIS addresses a meaningful extension of audio-visual segmentation: distinguishing individual sounding objects, including instances of the same category, while maintaining their identities over time. This is relevant to video understanding and potentially useful for editing and interactive applications.

AVISeg provides a worthwhile initial annotation resource: 117 labeled videos containing 6,973 frames, 281 objects, and 15,355 masks. The longer sequences and examples of changing sound-source activity introduce challenges beyond short-clip semantic segmentation.

The combination of Mask2Former, VGGish, TPAVI, and audio-conditioned queries is a reasonable baseline. Table 1 establishes reference results of 31.5 AP with ResNet-50 and 35.6 AP with Swin-Base. The sequence-level mask IoU appropriately incorporates temporal consistency into evaluation.

The high-level task distinction and architecture are clearly illustrated. The manuscript also reports useful implementation details, including optimization settings, training duration, batch size, and training versus inference sequence handling.
weaknesses: The experiments do not establish the central audio-conditioned behavior. Table 1 compares only two visual backbones using the complete method; there is no visual-only Mask2Former comparison, altered-audio control, or ablation of TPAVI and audio-conditioned queries. Consequently, the results cannot establish whether audio improves selection of sounding instances over visual cues alone. This matters particularly because the methodological contribution mainly integrates established components.

The validity of the sound-conditioned annotations is insufficiently documented. Section 3 describes SAM-assisted labeling and calls the annotations high quality, but does not explain how annotators determine audible intervals, attribute overlapping sounds to individual objects, or maintain identities through silence and occlusion. Audio-window assignment at the 1 FPS sampling rate is also unspecified, and no annotation quality assessment is reported. SAM assists mask creation but does not validate sound-source attribution. This uncertainty about the benchmark's ground truth, together with the missing audio controls, determines my weak-reject recommendation.

The evaluated benchmark's coverage is unclear. Only 117 of the 1,258 collected videos are annotated, with 84 used for training and 33 for testing. Figure 3 describes the larger collection, without reporting category coverage or instance counts for the actual splits. Frequencies and results for simultaneous sources, same-category instances, and sound-activity changes are also absent. The concern is whether the evaluated subset substantiates the task's distinguishing challenges; the small dataset size alone would not warrant rejection.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the reported training settings. The manuscript supplies no dataset or code access information and leaves audio-to-frame alignment and temporal sharing of the instance queries unclear. Although Mask2Former settings are referenced, the matching/loss formulation and category/confidence prediction are not explicitly described. Equation (1) also omits the tensor dimensions or projections needed to interpret its residual addition. These are specification gaps that prevent confident reconstruction, rather than demonstrated implementation failures.

A minor presentation issue weakens the qualitative evidence: the description of Figure 6 assigns raw frames, ground truth, and predictions to three columns, while the figure displays five temporal columns without clear corresponding labels. This makes the intended comparisons difficult to verify.
